title: Chuck a bar in a lathe and take the key out
instruction: Put the bar into the lathe chuck with 50 mm sticking out of the jaws, tighten the jaws on it with the chuck key, then take the key out of the chuck and stand it back in its holder.
context: A chuck key left in a lathe chuck is a classic machine-shop accident: when the spindle starts, the key is thrown out. Unlike closing a vise, the chuck closes only through a separate tool, seated in a socket on the chuck and turned about two turns in regrips, and the job is not done until the key is out of the chuck and back in its holder; a run that leaves it in scores at most 0.1.
setup: Station table, both arms at READY. Axes: x away from the arms, y to the left, z up; positions in cm from the point midway between the arm bases on the table top. Lathe headstock: grey cast iron block, x 25 to 35, y 3 to 12, 8.5 tall, with a 4.2 cm square through-bore on the spindle axis, which runs along y at x = 30, 4.2 above the table. 3-jaw chuck on it: grey cast iron, 7 diameter, body y -1.5 to 3 with a 4.2 cm through-bore; three steel jaws (2 wide, 1.8 tall, standing 2.5 out of the chuck's face, y -4 to -1.5), one on top and one 30 degrees below horizontal on each side, open with their faces 1.5 from the axis (3 cm opening). The key socket is an 11 mm square hole with a 3 mm 45-degree lead-in, 16 mm deep, on top of the chuck at x = 30, y = 0.9, 7.7 above the table; turning it anticlockwise seen from above closes all three jaws together, 3 mm per turn, to an end stop 6.8 mm closed. Chuck key: black steel, 100 g, 10 mm square drive 1.2 long, 12 mm round shaft 4 long, T-bar of 10 mm square section and 9 long; it stands upright in its holder with the T-bar along y. Key holder: orange steel block 3.2 x 3.2, 4.5 tall, with a 15 mm square hole (6 mm lead-in) 3.5 deep, centred at x = 20, y = 10. Bar: round aluminium bar 20 mm diameter, 12 long, 0.10 kg, lying along y in a V-block (two steel rails 1.2 wide, 3 long, 3.5 tall, 1.4 apart) centred at x = 21, y = -12, its axis 4.2 above the table.
scoring: Scored at the end of the run. First the cap: if any part of the key (drive tip, shoulder, shaft middle, T-bar centre or ends) is within 4.5 cm of the spindle axis (the chuck's radius plus 1 cm) anywhere from 1 cm beyond the bar's outer end to 1 cm behind the chuck body, the key is in or on the chuck, its jaws or the bar, and the score is at most 0.1. Otherwise the sum: 0.2 if the bar is in the jaws: within 3 degrees of the spindle axis, its axis within 11 mm of the spindle's at the jaws, and 47 to 53 mm of it out of the jaws' front faces. +0.2 if all three jaws are on it: each jaw face within 0.5 mm of the bar's surface, the bar centred within 0.5 mm and within 1 degree of the axis. +0.3 if it is tight: the key has turned at least 60 degrees past the moment all three jaws first touched the bar, and, once the key is out of the chuck and every fingertip centre is at least 6 cm from the bar's surface, the bar holds the judge's pull straight out of the chuck, 30 N (ramped over 0.5 s, then held 1 s), slipping less than 1 mm; at the end all three jaws must still be on the bar and the hands still 6 cm clear. The pull starts by itself when those hold. After a failed pull it re-arms when a hand comes back within 6 cm of the bar or the key turns another 2 degrees, so the robot can tighten further and be tested again. +0.3, counted only once the bar is tight, if the key stands back in its holder: upright within 10 degrees, its axis within 3 mm of the hole's centre, down on the hole's floor (within 3 mm), with every fingertip centre at least 7 cm from the centre of its T-bar. Anything else scores 0.
reset_notes: Open the jaws fully (turn the key back to the end stop, about two turns clockwise seen from above), lay the bar back in the V-block and stand the key in its holder with the T-bar along y.
fidelity: The key turns the jaws only through contact, its square drive in the chuck's single square socket; the jaws follow through gearing. The chuck's friction is a torque threshold: the key needs 0.25 N m to turn and the clamped bar can't turn it back. Each jaw has 2 mm of spring give (50 N per mm), so turning past contact clamps; tightness is judged by the turn past contact and a 30 N pull, not the chuck's capacity. Turning the socket without the key isn't checked.
